```{r setup}
library(symcompR)
x <- Symbol("x"); y <- Symbol("y")
```

This vignette covers `sympy.tensor.array` ($N$-dimensional arrays),
`sympy.tensor.tensor` (abstract index notation), `sympy.tensor.indexed`, and
the canonicalization algorithms of `sympy.combinatorics.tensor_can`.

## Arrays

`Array(data, shape)` is an $N$-dimensional array of expressions, filled in
row major order as in SymPy. `arr_get()` reads an entry, with indices
starting at 1 as usual in R. The helper below collects the entries of a one
or two dimensional array into an R character vector or matrix for display.

```{r}
entries <- function(a) {
  s <- shape(a)
  if (length(s) == 1) return(vapply(seq_len(s), function(i) sstr(arr_get(a, i)), ""))
  outer(seq_len(s[1]), seq_len(s[2]),
        Vectorize(function(i, j) sstr(arr_get(a, c(i, j)))))
}
M <- Array(list(1, 2, 3, 4), c(2, 2))
shape(M)
entries(M)
arr_get(M, c(1, 2))
entries(tensorproduct(Array(list(1, 2)), Array(list(x, y))))
tensorcontraction(M, c(1, 2))
entries(permutedims(M, c(2, 1)))
```

`derive_by_array()` differentiates with respect to an array of variables, so
applying it twice gives the Hessian.

```{r}
g <- derive_by_array(x^2 * y, list(x, y))
entries(g)
entries(derive_by_array(g, list(x, y)))
```

`tensordiagonal()` takes the diagonal over pairs of axes, and
`NDimArray()` is another name for `Array()`.

```{r}
C4 <- Array(as.list(1:16), c(2, 2, 2, 2))
entries(tensordiagonal(Array(list(1, 2, 3, 4), c(2, 2)), c(1, 2)))
shape(tensordiagonal(C4, c(1, 2), c(3, 4)))
shape(NDimArray(list(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), c(2, 3)))
```

### Transforms over subset lattices

`walsh_hadamard_transform()` and the Mobius transforms of
`sympy.discrete.transforms` work on sequences indexed by subsets:

```{r}
walsh_hadamard_transform(list(1, 2, 3, 4))
mobius_transform(list(1, 2, 3, 4))
inverse_mobius_transform(list(1, 3, 4, 10))
```

### Contraction structure of indexed expressions

`get_contraction_structure()` finds the summation indices of an expression
built from `Indexed` objects, and `format_contraction_structure()` makes the
result readable.

```{r}
i <- Idx("i"); j <- Idx("j")
A <- IndexedBase("A"); B <- IndexedBase("B")
format_contraction_structure(get_contraction_structure(A(i, j) * B(j)))
format_contraction_structure(get_contraction_structure(A(i, i)))
Indexed(A, i)
```

## Tensor index notation

`TensorIndexType()` declares a kind of index (with a metric), and
`TensorHead()` declares a tensor with given symmetries. Expressions follow
the Einstein summation convention: a repeated upper and lower index is
summed, and a minus sign marks a lower index. `canon_bp()` brings an
expression to canonical form, which detects symmetry cancellations.

```{r}
L <- TensorIndexType("L", dummy_name = "L")
idx <- tensor_indices("i, j", L)
i <- idx$i; j <- idx$j
A <- TensorHead("A", list(L, L), TensorSymmetry.fully_symmetric(-2))
B <- TensorHead("B", list(L, L), TensorSymmetry.fully_symmetric(2))
p <- TensorHead("p", list(L))
canon_bp(A(i, j) * B(-j, -i))
canon_bp(B(i, j) - B(j, i))
contract_metric(L$metric(i, j) * p(-j), L$metric)
```

The contraction of an antisymmetric tensor with a symmetric one vanishes,
and contracting with the metric raises the index of `p`.


### Building tensor expressions

`TensorIndex()` creates a single index, and `tensor_heads()` several tensor
heads at once. `TensMul()`, `TensAdd()`, and `tensor_mul()` build products
and sums explicitly. `get_free_indices()` and `get_dummy_indices()` report
the free and contracted indices.

```{r}
k <- TensorIndex("k", L)
k
hp <- tensor_heads("q, r", list(L))
q <- hp[[1]]; r <- hp[[2]]
e <- tensor_mul(q(i), r(-i), p(j))
e
get_free_indices(e)
get_dummy_indices(e)
TensAdd(q(i), r(i))
doit(TensMul(2, q(i)))
substitute_indices(q(i) * r(j), list(i, k))
```

### Symmetries

`TensorSymmetry()` describes the symmetry of a tensor through a base and
strong generating set. `TensorSymmetry.no_symmetry()`,
`TensorSymmetry.direct_product()`, and `TensorSymmetry.riemann()` cover the
common cases.

```{r}
TensorSymmetry.no_symmetry(2)
TensorSymmetry.direct_product(2, -2)
Rm <- TensorHead("R", rep(list(L), 4), TensorSymmetry.riemann())
TensorSymmetry(get_symmetric_group_sgs(2))
```

The Riemann tensor satisfies the cyclic identity
$R_{ijkl} + R_{iklj} + R_{iljk} = 0$, which `riemann_cyclic_replace()` and
`riemann_cyclic()` use to rewrite it:

```{r}
idx4 <- tensor_indices("m0, m1, m2, m3", L)
riemann_cyclic_replace(Rm(idx4$m0, idx4$m2, idx4$m1, idx4$m3))
riemann_cyclic(Rm(i, j, k, idx4$m0) * (Rm(-i, -j, -k, -idx4$m0) -
                                     2 * Rm(-i, -k, -j, -idx4$m0)))
```

### Kronecker delta

`contract_delta()` contracts the Kronecker delta of an index type:

```{r}
Ln <- TensorIndexType("Ln", dim = 3)
d <- tensor_indices("a, b", Ln)
Ln$delta
contract_delta(Ln$delta(d$a, -d$b) * Ln$delta(d$b, -d$a), Ln$delta)
```

### Partial derivatives

`PartialDerivative()` is the derivative of a tensor expression with respect
to a tensor. `pd_perform_derivative()` evaluates it and `pd_expand()`
distributes it over sums.

```{r}
Af <- TensorHead("Af", list(L))
pd <- PartialDerivative(Af(i), Af(j))
get_free_indices(pd)
pd_perform_derivative(pd)
pd_expand(PartialDerivative(Af(i) + q(i), Af(j)))
```

### Replacing tensors with arrays

`replace_with_arrays()` evaluates an expression once the components of each
tensor and of the metric are known. Here $H^{i}{}_{j}$ has the given
components and the metric is $\mathrm{diag}(1, -1)$.

```{r}
H <- TensorHead("H", list(L, L))
repl <- list(list(H(i, -j), Array(list(list(1, 2), list(3, 4)))),
             list(L, Array(list(list(1, 0), list(0, -1)))))
entries(replace_with_arrays(H(i, j), repl))
entries(replace_with_arrays(H(i, j), repl, list(i, -j)))
```

`TensorManager` holds the commutation rules between tensor groups:

```{r}
class(TensorManager)
```

## Canonicalization of tensor expressions

The `tensor_can` functions implement the Butler-Portugal algorithm that
`canon_bp()` uses. A tensor expression is encoded as a permutation of index
slots, and the symmetries as base and strong generating sets.
`get_symmetric_group_sgs()` gives the BSGS of a symmetric or antisymmetric
tensor, and `riemann_bsgs` that of the Riemann tensor.

```{r}
sgs2 <- get_symmetric_group_sgs(2)
sgs2
get_symmetric_group_sgs(3, antisym = TRUE)
riemann_bsgs
```

`canonicalize(g, dummies, msym, ...)` returns the canonical form of the
permutation `g`. The example is $A^{d_0 d_1} B_{d_1 d_0}$ written with slot
order $(2, 1, 3, 0)$ and two signature slots, for symmetric $A$ and $B$.

```{r}
P <- function(...) Permutation(c(...))
canonicalize(P(2, 1, 3, 0, 4, 5), 0:3, 0, list(sgs2[[1]], sgs2[[2]], 1, 0),
             list(sgs2[[1]], sgs2[[2]], 1, 0))
canonical_free(integer(), sgs2[[2]], P(1, 0, 2, 3), 2)
```

The helpers build the BSGS of products and of the dummy index symmetries:

```{r}
tensor_gens(sgs2[[1]], sgs2[[2]], list(0, 1), 0)
gens_products(list(sgs2[[1]], sgs2[[2]], list(0, 1), 0))
bsgs_direct_product(sgs2[[1]], sgs2[[2]], sgs2[[1]], sgs2[[2]])
dummy_sgs(0:3, 0, 4)
perm_af_direct_product(list(c(1, 0, 2, 3), c(0, 1, 3, 2)), list(c(1, 0)), 0)
get_minimal_bsgs(c(1, 0), list(P(0, 2, 1, 3, 4), P(1, 0, 2, 3, 4)))
```

`get_transversals()` and `transversal2coset()` list the coset
representatives along a base, and `double_coset_can_rep()` finds the
canonical representative of a double coset.

```{r}
sgs3 <- get_symmetric_group_sgs(3)
tr <- get_transversals(sgs3[[1]], sgs3[[2]])
length(tr)
transversal2coset(5, sgs3[[1]], tr)
dg <- dummy_sgs(0:5, 0, 6)
double_coset_can_rep(list(0:5), list(0), c(0, 2), dg,
                     get_transversals(c(0, 2), dg), P(4, 1, 3, 0, 5, 2, 6, 7))
```
